msk.lead: In the clinic, the prescription for muscle and joint pain almost always has the same backbone — **pain relief (acetaminophen) + anti-inflammatory (anti-inflammatory painkiller) + muscle relaxant + stomach protection**. Once you know why each slot is there, you can choose at the pharmacy using the same logic. Sudden low back pain mostly gets better on its own within a few weeks (American College of Physicians 2017), so medicine is a tool to help you keep moving in the meantime.
msk.planLabel: You can pick only the slots you need. Use just one anti-inflammatory — the pharmacy muscle-relaxant combination takes the place of the anti-inflammatory.

plan.title: Base pain relief — acetaminophen
plan.why: It lays down a floor of pain relief without straining your stomach or heart. On its own it doesn't work for low back pain (a large back-pain trial), but used **together with** an anti-inflammatory, the two work better than either alone (an analysis pooling several studies: when 3 people use it, about 2 benefit).

plan.title: Calm the inflammation — one anti-inflammatory painkiller
plan.why: The medicine with the strongest evidence for sudden low back pain and sprains (a strong recommendation from the American College of Physicians). If your stomach is sensitive, low-dose ibuprofen + famotidine; if your heart or blood pressure is a concern, naproxen. Whichever you choose, **only one**, after a meal.

plan.title: Loosen the knots — muscle relaxant
plan.why:
Use it when muscle knots or stiffness are clear. The effect is small but real (2021 pooled analysis), and eperisone is the standard prescription. At the pharmacy, the only option is a 3-ingredient combination with chlorzoxazone. If it makes you drowsy or keeps you awake, talk with your pharmacist about when to take it (some products contain caffeine).

Pharmacy muscle-relaxant combinations contain a pain-relief ingredient called **ethenzamide**, so the package insert says not to take them with other fever reducers and pain relievers or cold medicines. This product's package insert says not to take it at the same time as other fever reducers and pain relievers or cold medicines. Doctors sometimes use them together, but check with your pharmacist or doctor first before taking them together.

plan.title: Ease heartburn and stomach upset — famotidine
plan.why: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid,** keep over-the-counter famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use an anti-inflammatory — if you've had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from a doctor is the surer route. Everyone else can add it only when you have heartburn, and see a doctor if the heartburn keeps going. Over-the-counter famotidine is **a medicine that reduces heartburn** — it has not been shown that this dose prevents stomach bleeding or ulcers from anti-inflammatories. Antacids (such as aluminum phosphate gel) have no evidence for preventing ulcers.

how: **On the first day**, after a meal, take 1–2 acetaminophen tablets and one 400 mg ibuprofen tablet **together** (the package insert says not to take it with other fever reducers and pain relievers — doctors sometimes use them together, so check with your pharmacist before combining). After about 6 hours you can take another dose.

If the knots are bad, add a muscle-relaxant combination. This product's package insert says not to take it at the same time as other fever reducers and pain relievers or cold medicines. Doctors sometimes use them together, but check with your pharmacist or doctor first. If it makes you drowsy or keeps you awake, talk with your pharmacist about when to take it (some products contain caffeine). For stomach protection, follow the “Stomach protection” section below.

**On day 2–3**, once the pain is under control, cut back the anti-inflammatory first and keep only the acetaminophen. The rule is to take anti-inflammatories for as short a time and at as low a dose as possible.
If only one spot hurts, like a knee or wrist, you can start with a gel you rub on (3–4 times a day) or an anti-inflammatory patch (1–2 a day) instead of an anti-inflammatory you swallow.
If you still need the anti-inflammatory for more than 5 days, or you don't feel any better after 1–2 weeks, see a doctor.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist: “I have muscle pain in my lower back (shoulder). My stomach is fine (or: my stomach is sensitive). I'd like acetaminophen and ibuprofen. If the knots are bad, a muscle-relaxant combination too. If I get heartburn, famotidine too.” Check with the pharmacist first whether the muscle-relaxant combination is OK to take with the anti-inflammatory.
First mention the medicines you take (blood pressure medicine, blood thinners, other painkillers), whether you are pregnant, and whether you've ever had a stomach ulcer.
If you have an anti-inflammatory prescribed by a doctor, show it and ask, “Please give me only things that don't overlap with this.”
selfcare: **Keep moving a little, even if it hurts.** Walking and doing housework as usual helps you recover faster than staying in bed (American College of Physicians 2017 guideline).
**Use warm compresses.** Studies show heat eases low back pain for about five days. But for the first two days right after a fresh strain, a cold pack to bring down swelling comes first.
If you've been sitting a long time, stand up and stretch your back every 30 minutes. If your shoulders or neck hurt, set your TV or screen at eye level.
Massage and stretching are good, but don't force a stretch into the painful range. A stretch that feels good is enough.
avoid: Don't take two anti-inflammatories together (for example, ibuprofen and naproxen, or naproxen and a combination painkiller containing isopropylantipyrine). They block the same enzyme, so the effect stays the same while the amount in your body doubles — and the strain on your stomach and kidneys grows as the amount goes up.
Taking anti-inflammatories on an empty stomach or with alcohol harms your stomach. Always take them after a meal.
Even if a medicine 'feels too weak,' don't double the dose at once. Adding a different type of medicine (acetaminophen) instead is safer and works better.
Putting a heat pack or electric blanket over a pain patch can cause burns.

notWorking.title: If the medicine isn't helping much
steps: First, check how you're taking it. Are you taking the anti-inflammatory after meals at the set dose, **together with** acetaminophen? For the first two days, taking it regularly on schedule works much better than taking a little here and there.

Add rather than switch. Switching to a different anti-inflammatory makes almost no difference. Adding a pain patch or warm compress works better. If the knots are bad, you can switch from the anti-inflammatory you swallow to a muscle-relaxant combination (just one of the two).
If you don't feel better after 1–2 weeks, or numbness travels down your leg or arm, see a doctor. Imaging, a prescription muscle relaxant, and physical therapy can help.
Low back pain lasting more than 4 weeks needs another look. At that stage, exercise therapy is needed.

faq.q: Can I take acetaminophen and ibuprofen together?
faq.a: In theory, taking them at the same time isn't recommended (package insert), but doctors sometimes use them together when pain isn't well controlled — keep to each medicine's own dosing interval and daily maximum. Used together, they work better than either alone for sudden pain (a 2013 pooled analysis of pain after tooth removal: with both, out of 100 people, 73 had their pain cut by more than half; with ibuprofen alone, out of 100 people, 52 did). In an emergency room study, this combination worked as well as an opioid painkiller.

faq.q: Do I really need a muscle relaxant?
faq.a: It's not essential. For sudden low back pain the effect is 'small but real,' and it causes drowsiness. Use it for just a few days when knots or stiffness are clear.

faq.q: When should I add stomach protection?
faq.a: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid,** keep over-the-counter famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use an anti-inflammatory — if you've had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from a doctor is the surer route. Everyone else can add it only when you have heartburn, and see a doctor if the heartburn keeps going. Over-the-counter famotidine is a medicine that reduces heartburn — it has not been shown that this dose prevents stomach bleeding from anti-inflammatories.

dysmenorrhea.lead:
Period pain comes from **the uterus contracting as if it's being wrung out**. So medicine is used in two ways.

**An anti-inflammatory painkiller** is the 1st choice (not acetaminophen). It reduces the very substance that causes the pain — in an analysis pooling 80 trials, it worked more than 4 times better than a placebo, and better than acetaminophen too.

You can add **an antispasmodic that relaxes the contractions** (the evidence is weak).

And **timing is half the battle** — start when the pain begins, or from the day before, and take it regularly by the clock.
dysmenorrhea.planLabel: The key: one anti-inflammatory, taken 'early and regularly'

plan.title: 1st choice — one anti-inflammatory painkiller
plan.why: It reduces the very substance that causes the pain, so for period pain this comes first. **Take a full dose as soon as the pain starts**, and for the first 2–3 days take it regularly by the clock. If you wait and hold out, it works less well. Take it after eating.

plan.title: Something you can add — an antispasmodic that relaxes contractions (weak evidence)
plan.why:
Period pain comes from **the uterus contracting as if it's being wrung out**. Butylscopolamine relaxes those contractions, so you **can try adding it** to an anti-inflammatory painkiller — but the evidence that it helps period pain is weak, and the 1st choice is the anti-inflammatory painkiller.

Pharmacies also carry combination tablets that put a pain-relief ingredient in the same pill. **If you have glaucoma or an enlarged prostate,** avoid it.

plan.title: Add-on — acetaminophen
plan.why: Doctors add this when the anti-inflammatory alone isn't enough. In theory, taking them at the same time isn't recommended (package insert), but they are sometimes used together and work better than either alone — keep to each medicine's own dosing interval and daily maximum. If you take a combination product, check whether it already contains acetaminophen.

plan.title: If your stomach is sensitive while using an anti-inflammatory — famotidine
plan.why: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid,** keep over-the-counter famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use an anti-inflammatory — if you've had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from a doctor is the surer route. Everyone else can add it only when you have heartburn, and see a doctor if the heartburn keeps going.

plan.title: If it disrupts your life every month — hormone treatment
plan.why: Instead of getting through each period with painkillers, this **reduces the cause of the pain**. Birth control pills or a hormonal device reduce menstrual flow and the contractions themselves. A doctor will also check for endometriosis or fibroids.

how: When you feel signs that your period is starting (a heavy lower back, an aching lower belly), take the first dose **right away**: 2 naproxen capsules or 400 mg of ibuprofen. If your pain comes regularly every month, you can start the day before your period is due.

After that, take only one of the two — either naproxen, 1 capsule every 6–8 hours, or ibuprofen, 400 mg every 6–8 hours (2 tablets if each is 200 mg) — **on schedule for the first 2–3 days**, whether or not it hurts. Don't take the two together.

If that's still not enough, doctors sometimes add 1 acetaminophen tablet in between — in theory taking them at the same time isn't recommended, so keep to each medicine's own dosing interval and daily maximum.
The daily maximums are naproxen 1,250 mg, ibuprofen 1,200 mg (for over-the-counter use), and acetaminophen 4 g.
Using a warm compress on your belly and lower back at the same time works about as well as the medicine.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist: “I have period pain. I'd like naproxen or ibuprofen. And famotidine too, if my stomach is sensitive.”
Mention any stomach ulcer, asthma, chance of pregnancy, and whether you take a blood thinner.
selfcare: **Keep your lower belly warm.** When several studies were pooled, heat worked about as well as painkillers.
**Exercise steadily day to day.** People who exercised regularly had noticeably less period pain (an analysis pooling several studies).
A low-frequency nerve stimulator may also help. The evidence isn't solid yet, but it does no harm.
Ginger tea helped in small studies. Think of it only as an add-on.
avoid: Don't 'hold out as long as you can' before taking it. By then the pain substances (prostaglandins) are already made, so it works less well. Take it as soon as you see the first signs.

Don't double up on two anti-inflammatories (for example, naproxen with a combination painkiller containing isopropylantipyrine, or two different period-pain products that each contain an anti-inflammatory).
Anti-inflammatories taken on an empty stomach or with alcohol harm your stomach.
Taking a caffeine-containing combination painkiller on many days every month can actually bring on headaches caused by the medicine itself.

notWorking.title: If the medicine isn't helping much
steps: First, check when and how much you're taking. As soon as it starts, a slightly bigger first dose, then regularly on schedule — sticking to just these three usually makes a difference.
Add acetaminophen and use a warm compress as well.
If after 3–6 months of this your daily life is still hard every month, see a gynecologist. Hormone treatment (such as birth control pills) and checks for endometriosis or adenomyosis can help a lot.

If you have pain on days you're not on your period, pain during sex, a sudden increase in menstrual flow, or severe period pain for the first time after age 25, there may be another cause. Please see a doctor.

faq.q: Doesn't acetaminophen work for period pain?
faq.a: It works, but it's weaker than anti-inflammatories (an analysis pooling several studies: anti-inflammatory painkillers worked about 2 times as well). For people who can't take anti-inflammatories (after 20 weeks of pregnancy, with a stomach ulcer, or with asthma triggered by these medicines), it's the 1st choice.

faq.q: Which is better: naproxen, ibuprofen or dexibuprofen?
faq.a: They work equally well. Naproxen's strengths are an approved larger first dose and a longer-lasting effect; ibuprofen and dexibuprofen are easier on the stomach.

faq.q: Do birth control pills help period pain?
faq.a: Yes. Guidelines list them as the 2nd-line treatment after anti-inflammatory painkillers (American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists). They need a prescription, and they reduce pain by stopping ovulation.

headache.lead: Most headaches are tension-type or migraine, and ordinary painkillers can handle them. The rules: **one full dose early on**, and **no more than 10–15 days a month** — taking painkillers often can itself cause 'medication-overuse headache' (International Classification of Headache Disorders). A headache that comes on suddenly like a thunderclap needs the emergency room, not medicine.
headache.planLabel: Two single-ingredient medicines beat a combination painkiller

plan.title: Acetaminophen or ibuprofen
plan.why: Start here for tension-type headache or migraine. For migraine, **anti-inflammatories work a little better** (ibuprofen 400 mg, naproxen 500 mg). One tip: **don't hold out and take a little at a time — take one full dose when it hurts**.

plan.title: If it's not enough — both types together
plan.why: If one isn't enough, try **acetaminophen and ibuprofen together**. They work better than either alone (the package insert says not to take it with other fever reducers and pain relievers — doctors sometimes use them together, so check with your pharmacist before combining). Caffeine-containing combination painkillers help a little more too, but taking them **more than ten days a month** pushes you toward headaches caused by the medicine. The combination with acetaminophen, ethenzamide and caffeine says in its package insert not to take it with other painkillers, so take that one on its own.

plan.title: Muscle relaxant — if your neck and shoulders are tight
plan.why:
**Tension-type headache and migraine often come mixed together rather than separately.** When neck and shoulder muscles are knotted hard as a rock, the pain climbs from the back of the neck into the head. Doctors sometimes give a muscle relaxant for this, but **European headache guidelines don't recommend muscle relaxants for tension-type headache.** Try a 10-minute warm compress and neck and shoulder stretches first.

Pharmacies carry combination products with chlorzoxazone, and doctors use eperisone. If it makes you drowsy or keeps you awake, talk with your pharmacist about when to take it (some products contain caffeine).

Pharmacy muscle-relaxant combinations contain a pain-relief ingredient called **ethenzamide**, so the package insert says not to take them with other fever reducers and pain relievers or cold medicines. This product's package insert says not to take it at the same time as other fever reducers and pain relievers or cold medicines. Doctors sometimes use them together, but check with your pharmacist or doctor first before taking them together.

plan.title: When your stomach is upset — protect and settle it
plan.why:
Many people get heartburn from headache medicine, and **migraine itself often brings nausea**.

If an anti-inflammatory gives you heartburn, try over-the-counter **famotidine** (up to 20 mg a day) with it — if the heartburn keeps going or doesn't improve, see a doctor. If you feel bloated, as if food is stuck, **trimebutine** can help. If you feel so sick you can't even swallow pills, get an anti-nausea medicine from a doctor as well.

plan.title: If the headache came at the end of a cold — check your nose first
plan.why:
A headache at the end of a cold is a different kind.

If it comes with a runny or stuffy nose and **your forehead or cheekbones feel heavy, and it hurts more when you bend your head down** — headache medicine alone usually won't do it. The pain comes from blocked hollow spaces beside the nose (the sinuses), so **clearing your nose is the headache treatment**.

Rinse your nose with saline and try a decongestant nasal spray for no more than three days. See the [[symptom:rhinitis|stuffy nose page]] too. If thick yellow mucus lasts more than ten days or the fever comes back, it's sinusitis, so see a doctor.

plan.title: Before switching medicine — first, which headache is it?
plan.why:
From here on these are prescription medicines, and **the right medicine depends completely on the kind of headache.** First see which kind yours is.

**Squeezing on both sides, like a band around your head** → tension-type. The painkillers above plus neck and shoulder stretches are the basics.

**Throbbing on one side, light and sound bother you, and you feel sick** → migraine. The prescription medicines below change life for many people.

If it hurts **on four or more days a month** or you take **painkillers on ten or more days a month** → that itself is the problem. Marking headache days and medicine days on a calendar and showing it to your doctor is the fastest way.

plan.title: If it's migraine — triptans (when an attack starts)
plan.why:
Made specifically for migraine, they're in a different league from ordinary painkillers. **Taking them early, as the pain starts**, is the key.

There are several, such as sumatriptan, rizatriptan and naratriptan, and the right one differs from person to person, so **when one doesn't work, another often does**. People who have had heart disease or a stroke don't use them.

plan.title: If it comes often — a daily preventive medicine
plan.why:
If you get migraine on more than four days a month, you move to **a medicine taken every day to cut how often it comes, not one taken when it hurts**.

These include flunarizine, propranolol, topiramate and amitriptyline, and **you need to try them for two to three months** to judge whether they work. With a preventive, you take painkillers on fewer days, which also helps you get out of medication-overuse headache.

how: When a headache starts, take ibuprofen 400 mg (or 2 acetaminophen tablets) with water. If you wait and hold out, it works less well.

If nothing has changed after 1 hour, add a different type of medicine. If you took ibuprofen, add acetaminophen, for example (the package insert says not to take it with other fever reducers and pain relievers — doctors sometimes use them together, so check with your pharmacist before combining).
Drink two glasses of water and rest somewhere dark for just 20 minutes. Not enough water, not enough sleep, and skipping your usual coffee are common causes.
If you're taking painkillers on more than 10 days a month, don't increase them — see a doctor.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist: “I have a tension headache (or a headache that seems like migraine). I'd like ibuprofen and acetaminophen.”
If you tell the pharmacist how many days a month you take painkillers, they can screen for headaches caused by the medicine.
selfcare: Keep your sleep times, mealtimes and amount of coffee about the same every day. Stopping coffee suddenly can also bring on a headache.
Loosen up your neck and shoulders often, and keep TV and phone screens at eye level.
If you have migraines, jot down when it hurt and whether it was linked to sleep, your period, certain foods or stress. It helps a lot at your doctor's visit.
avoid: Don't take caffeine-containing combination painkillers every day out of habit.
Taking a lot of acetaminophen for a hangover headache strains your liver. Water and rest come first; if needed, a small dose of ibuprofen after eating.
Don't double the same medicine because 'one tablet didn't work.'

notWorking.title: If the medicine isn't helping much
steps: Have you tried a full dose from the start, with both types (acetaminophen + an anti-inflammatory) together? A cup of coffee can also boost the effect (don't let it become a habit).
If you feel queasy, light bothers you, and one side throbs, it's likely migraine. Many people find life changes when they switch to a prescription medicine called a triptan.

If you have headaches on more than 15 days a month and take painkillers on more than 10–15 days, that's 'medication-overuse headache.' It gets better by cutting back the medicine, and you should do this with a doctor.
If you have even one of the 'doctor / emergency room' signs below, get seen right away instead of taking medicine.

faq.q: Isn't a combination painkiller with caffeine and isopropylantipyrine the best for headaches?
faq.a: It's fast, but the evidence says the acetaminophen + ibuprofen combination is stronger, and that product carries warnings that it's not for children under 15 and shouldn't be taken for long. Now and then is fine, but for your medicine cabinet, two single-ingredient medicines are better.

faq.q: I've heard taking headache medicine often is bad. How often is too often?
faq.a: **Ten days a month** is the line. Take it more often and the medicine itself starts causing headaches (medication-overuse headache). Caffeine-containing combinations get you there faster. Just mark 'medicine days' on a calendar and you'll see quickly — if you go over ten days, it's not time to switch medicines but **time to talk about a preventive medicine**.

faq.q: How do I know if a headache comes from tight neck and shoulders?
faq.a: **Press the back of your neck and the tops of your shoulders with your hand.** If they're hard as a rock and pressing feels 'good,' that's the kind. Try a 10-minute warm compress and neck and shoulder stretches first. Doctors sometimes give a muscle relaxant too, but European headache guidelines don't recommend muscle relaxants for tension-type headache. Pharmacy muscle-relaxant combinations contain a pain-relief ingredient, so their package insert says not to take them with other painkillers — choose **just one of the two**, the painkiller or the combination. If you feel you really need both, talk with your pharmacist (they are sometimes used together when needed).

sorethroat.lead: Most sore throats are viral, so antibiotics aren't needed, and **pain control** is the treatment. Anti-inflammatory lozenges you dissolve in your mouth (flurbiprofen) gave first relief in as little as 11 minutes, and acetaminophen or ibuprofen by mouth also work well. If it's severe for more than 3 days, or you have a fever or pus on your tonsils, see a doctor.
sorethroat.planLabel: One that works on the throat + one you swallow — often either one is enough

plan.title: Flurbiprofen lozenge — goes straight to the sore throat
plan.why:
A lozenge containing flurbiprofen. **Don't swallow it — let it dissolve slowly in your mouth** so the medicine reaches the sore throat directly. It brings relief faster than a medicine you swallow. Every 3–6 hours, up to 5 a day, for no more than 3 days.

Use it so it **doesn't overlap** with an anti-inflammatory you swallow (such as ibuprofen). If you need a medicine by mouth for fever or body aches, use acetaminophen alongside it.

plan.title: Painkiller by mouth — alongside the lozenge
plan.why: If you also have fever or body aches, use a medicine you swallow. The lozenge is an anti-inflammatory too, so with ibuprofen you have to think about your total anti-inflammatory dose — in that case, choose acetaminophen.

plan.title: If it hurts a lot — benzydamine gargle (pharmacy)
plan.why: It reaches the throat directly and eases both the inflammation and the soreness. It's also used after tonsil surgery or when the mouth is sore from cancer drugs or radiation. **You can buy it at a pharmacy** — rinse with 15 mL undiluted for 20–30 seconds and spit it out, 2–3 times a day. Don't use it for more than 7 days without a doctor's advice.

plan.title: If it's bacterial tonsillitis — antibiotics (prescription)
plan.why: High fever + white pus on the tonsils + no cough + swollen glands under the jaw could mean a bacterial (strep) infection, so get checked — testing and antibiotics come from a doctor.

how: Slowly dissolve 1 lozenge (throat lozenge) every 3–6 hours. Don't chew it. Up to 5 a day, for no more than 3 days.
If you have a fever or body aches, take 1–2 acetaminophen tablets every 6 hours.
Warm water, honey tea, a humidifier, and salt-water gargles help.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist: “My throat hurts, especially when I swallow. I'd like an anti-inflammatory lozenge.”
Mention asthma, stomach ulcer, or pregnancy. The lozenges also contain an anti-inflammatory.

If it hurts so much that it's hard to swallow even with the lozenge, ask for a **benzydamine gargle** as well. You can buy it at a pharmacy, and since you rinse and spit it out, it's easy on your stomach.
selfcare: A spoonful of honey soothes throat irritation and cough (for children past their first birthday).
Rest your voice and stay away from cigarette smoke.
Sip water little and often. Warm tea is good too.
avoid: Don't stack ibuprofen and a combination painkiller containing isopropylantipyrine on top of a throat lozenge. That doubles up the anti-inflammatories.
Don't take leftover antibiotics you have at home on your own.

notWorking.title: If the medicine isn't helping much
steps: If it's still hard to swallow after 3 days, get checked for tonsillitis or pharyngitis at a clinic.
If one side is badly swollen and you can't open your mouth well, pus may have collected beside the tonsil. Get medical care right away, the same day.

faq.q: How can I tell if my throat needs antibiotics?
faq.a: **Fever, white pus on the tonsils, tender glands under the jaw, and no cough** — the more of these four you have, the more likely it's bacterial (strep), and you need a test. On the other hand, if a cough, runny nose or hoarse voice comes with it, it's mostly viral and antibiotics won't help.

faq.q: Can I keep eating throat lozenges like candy?
faq.a: Flurbiprofen lozenges are **anti-inflammatories**, so take up to 5 a day, 3–6 hours apart, for no more than 3 days. Taking them with other anti-inflammatories such as ibuprofen or a combination painkiller containing isopropylantipyrine strains your stomach.

faq.q: Do salt-water gargles help?
faq.a: The evidence is weak, but they're harmless and many people find them soothing. Dissolve half a teaspoon of salt in a cup of lukewarm water, rinse for 30 seconds and spit it out. Don't swallow it.

cold.lead: Medicine doesn't cure a cold — it gets better on its own over 7–10 days, and medicine is a tool to make that time less miserable. So the clinic way is to **choose by 'what job do I want this medicine to do,' not by the name of the symptom** — bring down fever and aches, calm inflammation, protect the stomach, thin mucus. Below is that clinic combination **translated into ingredients you can buy at a pharmacy**.
cold.planTitle: Colds — how to choose at the pharmacy
cold.planLabel: Here's the clinic combination translated into pharmacy ingredients

plan.title: Acetaminophen — for aches and fever
plan.why: The basic choice when you have a fever and ache all over. It's fine on an empty stomach and rarely clashes with medicines you already take. In Korea, you can even get it at convenience stores.

plan.title: Everything in one bottle — liquid multi-symptom cold medicine
plan.why: If fever, runny nose and cough all hit at once, this one bottle covers it. But **it also contains acetaminophen.** If you also buy acetaminophen separately, **your daily amount doubles — choose just one.** It already has a runny-nose ingredient, so you can skip the 'Runny nose' slot below. One such liquid is taken by adults as one pouch (20 mL) three times a day — **children get a share by age** (age 2–3: 1/4 pouch, age 3–7: 1/3 pouch, age 7–11: 1/2 pouch, age 11–15: 2/3 pouch). Another is taken as one bottle (20 mL) three times a day. But multi-symptom cold medicines contain **a runny-nose ingredient that causes drowsiness and dry mouth**, so if you are over 65, choosing single-ingredient medicines is easier on your body.

plan.title: Ibuprofen (anti-inflammatory) — inflammation and fever together
plan.why: Better if your throat is swollen and sore or you ache all over. **It also calms the inflammation.** **In theory, taking it at the same time as acetaminophen isn't recommended** (package insert), but doctors sometimes use them together when symptoms aren't controlled — keep to each medicine's own dosing interval and daily maximum. Take it after eating.

plan.title: If your stomach is sensitive while using an anti-inflammatory — famotidine
plan.why: **If you are 65 or older, or also take a blood thinner or a steroid,** keep over-the-counter famotidine (up to 20 mg a day) alongside while you use an anti-inflammatory — if you've had a stomach ulcer, getting a prescription acid reducer from a doctor is the surer route. Everyone else can add it only when you have heartburn, and see a doctor if the heartburn keeps going.

plan.title: Acetylcysteine — thins mucus
plan.why: You can try it when mucus is sticky and won't come up. It's meant to **thin the mucus** so it's easier to cough up, but the evidence that mucus medicines help cold coughs is weak. You can buy it at a pharmacy. 200 mg at a time, three times a day. **Drinking water often matters as much as the medicine.**

plan.title: Runny or stuffy nose only — saline and nasal spray (antihistamine if you have allergies)
plan.why: **If you chose the multi-symptom cold medicine above, skip this slot** — it already has a runny-nose ingredient. This is only for people choosing single medicines. Non-drowsy allergy medicines (such as loratadine) haven't been shown to help a cold's runny nose. For a runny nose, saline rinses come first; loratadine helps only if you also have allergic rhinitis. For a stuffy nose, use **a nasal spray**. Use the spray for no more than three days — using it longer makes your nose more blocked.

plan.title: What doctors do — the clinic cold combination
plan.why:
The backbone is the same as the pharmacy combination. **There are two things only a doctor can add.**

One is **an antibiotic** (cefixime). Colds are viral, so antibiotics don't work on them. Doctors add one only when there are **signs that a bacterial infection has set in on top** — these are the four they look for.
· **No improvement after ten days**
· **Getting better, then worse again** — this is the clearest sign
· **A fever near 39°C and yellow mucus from the start, lasting three or four days**
· **Pain in one side of the face or cheekbone, or pus on the tonsils with swollen glands in the front of the neck and no cough**

On the other hand, **yellow mucus or phlegm alone is not a reason for antibiotics.** The color gets darker even as a cold is getting better. **Using them when they're not needed breeds resistance, so they won't work when a bacterial infection really does set in.** Knowing this, instead of 'please give me antibiotics,' you'll tell your doctor **'how many days it's been, and whether it got better then worse again'** — and that's far more useful information.

The other is **a cough syrup containing codeine**. It's used when a night-time cough keeps you from sleeping.

Everything else stays in the same slots — loxoprofen as the anti-inflammatory, and mosapride as well if your stomach feels bloated.

how: **In the daytime**, take acetaminophen only. For a runny nose, rinsing with saline comes first — non-drowsy allergy medicines such as loratadine haven't been shown to help a cold's runny nose, and help only if you also have allergic rhinitis. If your nose is blocked, use a nasal spray just once.

**At night**, take 1 dose of multi-symptom cold medicine. The drowsy ingredient helps you sleep. Multi-symptom cold medicine also contains acetaminophen, so leave out the separate acetaminophen at night — if you split them (acetaminophen by day, cold medicine at night), don't go over 4,000 mg of acetaminophen a day from both combined, and space them at least 4 hours apart (the package insert says not to take them together, so check with your pharmacist).
Drink 2 L of water a day, keep the room humid, and get plenty of sleep. If the fever lasts more than 3 days, see a doctor.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist your main symptom. If you say “I just have a runny nose / my nose is blocked / I just have body aches,” they'll pick only the ingredients that fit.
Be sure to mention if you have high blood pressure, prostate problems or glaucoma, are pregnant, or are over 65. Decongestants and antihistamines are the medicines to be careful with.
selfcare: Drink warm water and honey tea (for children past their first birthday) often, and keep the room humid.
If your nose is blocked and runny, rinse it with saline. It's a proven method.
Get plenty of rest. In the end, it's your own immune system that clears a cold.
avoid: If you take multi-symptom cold medicine plus acetaminophen plus a combination painkiller that also contains acetaminophen, you get acetaminophen three times over. Pick just one.
Adding a sleep aid or motion-sickness medicine to a multi-symptom cold medicine doubles up the drowsy ingredient (antihistamine).
Antibiotics don't work on colds. Colds are caused by viruses.
Don't give cold medicine to children under two. It doesn't work and carries only risk.

notWorking.title: If the medicine isn't helping much
steps: A cold usually lasts 7–10 days. Medicine makes that time easier; it doesn't end the cold.
If the fever lasts more than 3 days, symptoms go past ten days, or you get better and then worse again, see a doctor.
If you're short of breath, have chest pain, or have yellow phlegm together with a high fever, it could be pneumonia or the flu, so get checked. Don't put it off.

faq.q: Can I take a multi-symptom cold liquid and acetaminophen together?
faq.a: In Korea, 1 bottle of a common multi-symptom cold liquid already contains 300 mg of acetaminophen. So **don't take them at the same time.** If you split them (acetaminophen by day, cold medicine at night), don't go over 4,000 mg of acetaminophen a day from both combined, and space them at least 4 hours apart (the package insert says not to take them together, so check with your pharmacist).

faq.q: Shouldn't I get antibiotics for a cold?
faq.a:
Colds are viral, so **antibiotics don't work on them.** Yellow mucus or phlegm doesn't mean you need antibiotics either — the color gets darker as you get better.

Doctors add an antibiotic when there are **signs that a bacterial infection has set in on top**: no change after ten days, **getting better then worse again**, a fever near 39°C from the start lasting three or four days, or pain in one side of the face or cheekbone. Rather than 'please give me antibiotics,' telling your doctor **'how many days it's been, and whether it got better then worse again'** is far more useful information.

faq.q: Is one multi-symptom cold medicine enough, or are separate ones better?
faq.a:
**If you have several symptoms, one bottle is convenient; if you have one or two, single medicines are better.**

Multi-symptom cold medicines contain fever and pain, runny nose, stuffy nose and cough ingredients all together, so if you only have a runny nose you end up taking **ingredients you don't need**. Especially **if you are over 65**, the runny-nose ingredient can cause drowsiness, dry mouth and trouble passing urine, so choosing single medicines is easier on your body.

fever.lead: A fever isn't an illness itself but your body's response, so fever reducers are **'symptom control' that makes you more comfortable when it's hard** — they don't treat the cause. A lower temperature doesn't mean you're better, so **if it lasts more than 3 days, or comes down and then goes back up**, don't buy more medicine — go and find out the cause. For adults it's one medicine, acetaminophen or ibuprofen; for children, it all comes down to a dose based on weight.
fever.planLabel: One medicine if one is enough; both together if it's tough

plan.title: Acetaminophen 500–1,000 mg
plan.why: The 1st choice, with no strain on stomach or heart. If body aches are bad, ibuprofen 400 mg is good too.

plan.title: By weight — acetaminophen 10–15 mg/kg / ibuprofen 5–10 mg/kg
plan.why: Work it out by **weight**, not age. Acetaminophen every 4–6 hours, no more than 5 times a day (from 4 months old); ibuprofen every 6–8 hours (from 6 months old; avoid if dehydrated).

plan.title: If one isn't enough — sometimes together or alternating
plan.why: **In theory, taking the two at the same time isn't recommended** (package insert, UK guidelines), but when a fever won't come down, doctors sometimes use them together or alternate them. If you do, **keep each medicine's interval (acetaminophen 4 hours, ibuprofen 6 hours) and daily maximum separately**, and write down the time and medicine for each dose. Using both brings the fever down a little more (an analysis pooling several studies), but **giving extra by mistake because of mix-ups** is the most common accident.

how: Adults: with the Korean 500 mg acetaminophen tablets described here, take 1–2 tablets every 4–6 hours and don't go over 8 tablets (4 g) a day. Products elsewhere may contain a different amount per tablet or set a lower daily limit, so follow your own product's label.

For a child (for example, 10 kg), give children's acetaminophen syrup (160 mg/5 mL) 3–4.5 mL at a time, every 4–6 hours. Try the children's dose calculator, which works it out from your child's weight.
Dress them in light clothes and wipe them with a lukewarm damp cloth. Don't wipe with cold water or alcohol.
Drink water or an electrolyte drink often.
pharmacy: If you tell the pharmacist your child's weight, they'll work out the amount in mL.
Tell them about any medicine you've already given. Cold medicines contain fever-reducing ingredients too.
selfcare: Drink water often, get plenty of rest, and dress them in light clothes.
Write down the time and the temperature, and when you gave medicine. That's the most helpful thing at the doctor's visit.
avoid: Don't give aspirin to children under 15 (risk of Reye's syndrome). Combination painkillers containing isopropylantipyrine must not be given under 15 either, and children's fever reducers (acetaminophen or ibuprofen syrup) are a better fit than combination painkillers.
Giving a separate fever reducer on top of cold syrup doubles up the acetaminophen.
Don't use ibuprofen in babies under 6 months, or when a child is dehydrated from vomiting or diarrhea.
Don't give cold baths or alcohol rubs. They make the child shiver instead.

notWorking.title: If the fever won't come down with medicine
steps: Fever reducers only bring the temperature down by about 1–1.5°C. Even if the number doesn't come all the way down, if your child is playing and drinking, that's OK.
Check once more that the dose matches the weight (children's dose calculator).
If the fever goes past 3 days, or comes with any of the 'doctor / emergency room' signs below, get seen.

faq.q: Can I give the two together?
faq.a: **In theory, taking them at the same time isn't recommended** (package insert, UK guidelines). If one makes things comfortable, that's enough. But when a fever won't come down, doctors sometimes use them together or alternate them. If you do, **keep each medicine's interval and daily maximum separately**, and write down the times and medicines.

faq.q: At what temperature should I give medicine?
faq.a:
**How they look comes before the number.** Even at 38°C, if they're playing and drinking well, there's no need to hurry with medicine; even at 37.8°C, if they're limp and clearly uncomfortable, give it. Fever reducers are **not medicines that get rid of fever but medicines that ease the discomfort**.

But **a baby under 3 months with a temperature of 38°C or higher always needs a doctor**. There are no exceptions to this.

faq.q: If the fever won't come down, does that mean something serious?
faq.a:
If a fever reducer brings it down by **about 1–1.5°C**, that's a normal response. You don't need to worry that it doesn't drop all the way to 36°C.

What to watch isn't the number but **how they look** — if they stay limp even when woken, haven't passed urine for half a day or more, have a stiff neck, are short of breath, or have a rash that doesn't fade when pressed, that's when to see a doctor. **If the fever goes past three days**, find out the cause too.

cough.lead: Coughing is a reflex that clears your airways, so **if there's phlegm, don't stop it — thin it**, and **only suppress a dry cough when it's disturbing your sleep**. In an analysis pooling several studies, the evidence for ordinary cough medicines was weak, and honey, fluids and humidity do a similar job. A cough lasting more than 3 weeks may not be a cold.
cough.planLabel: Phlegm or no phlegm is the fork in the road

plan.title: If you have phlegm and a sore throat together
plan.why:
A common combination after a cold. If the phlegm is sticky, you can try **a medicine that thins phlegm (acetylcysteine)** (the evidence for cold coughs is weak), and if your throat hurts, add a painkiller. Mucus medicine only earns its keep if you drink plenty of water — once it thins the phlegm, there has to be water to push it out.

When there's a lot of phlegm, **water and humidity come before medicine that suppresses the cough**.

For mucus medicine, pick **just one** of the three — acetylcysteine three times a day, **erdosteine two or three times a day**, and ambroxol three times a day. If you tend to forget doses, the one taken fewer times is better.

plan.title: If sour liquid comes up and you feel bloated
plan.why:
**A cough from stomach acid coming up and irritating the throat** is more common than you'd think. If it's worse lying down, your voice is hoarse in the morning, and you have sour liquid, burping or burning under the breastbone, suspect this.

In that case, **a medicine that reduces stomach acid (famotidine)** is the answer, not cough medicine. Also avoid eating dinner late, don't lie down right after eating, and raise your pillow a little.

plan.title: If it feels like mucus is dripping down the back of your throat
plan.why: This cough comes from mucus from your nose irritating your throat. **Treating the nose** works faster than cough medicine. If it's worse before bed, this is the likely cause.

plan.title: If there's no phlegm but you can't sleep at night
plan.why:
Use cough-suppressing medicine (dextromethorphan) **only when there's no phlegm and you can't sleep**. If you suppress it when there's phlegm, the phlegm pools. Multi-symptom cold medicines contain the same ingredient, so check the box to avoid doubling up.

An analysis pooling several studies found ordinary cough medicines don't clearly work — **it's best to keep expectations a little lower**.

**How to choose** — if only the cough bothers you, **single-ingredient dextromethorphan**. If the cough comes with a runny nose and phlegm, one **combination syrup** — it makes you drowsy and **must not overlap** with other cold or runny-nose medicines. If your throat feels scratchy and prickly, **a herbal throat powder** — it contains licorice, so talk with your pharmacist or doctor if you have high blood pressure. **Pick just one cough medicine.**

plan.title: More than 3 weeks or wheezing — see a doctor
plan.why: See a doctor if it lasts more than 3 weeks, you're wheezing, you have yellow phlegm with fever or chest pain, or there's blood in it. If your airways have become oversensitive, an inhaler is the next step.

how: For **a cough with phlegm**, drink water often and keep the room humid, then take one of the phlegm-thinning medicines (acetylcysteine, erdosteine, ambroxol) 3 times a day. Guaifenesin in multi-symptom cold medicines has the same purpose but in a smaller amount, so if phlegm is your main symptom, a single-ingredient medicine is better.
For **a dry cough**, take 1 dose of dextromethorphan and a spoonful of honey (for children past their first birthday) before bed.
If the cough comes from mucus dripping down the back of your throat, allergy medicine and saline nose rinses are a better fit.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist clearly, “I have phlegm” or “It's a dry cough.”
If you take antidepressants, be sure to say so, since they can interact with dextromethorphan.
selfcare: Honey (for children past their first birthday), warm water and humidity soothe a cough.
Quit smoking, and stay away from other people's smoke too.
Raising your pillow a little at night cuts down coughs from mucus dripping down or stomach acid coming up.
avoid: Don't use cough-stopping medicine (cough suppressant) for a cough with phlegm. The phlegm needs to come out.
Never give honey to babies under one year old.
Don't give cold or cough medicine to children under two (package insert). For ages 2–4, US guidance also doesn't recommend it, so talk with a doctor or pharmacist before giving it.

notWorking.title: If the medicine isn't helping much
steps: A cough after a cold can last up to 3 weeks. Try not to worry too much.

See a doctor if it's been more than 3 weeks, or you wheeze and get short of breath at night, have blood in your phlegm, or have weight loss or drenching night sweats. Asthma, reflux, tuberculosis and pneumonia need to be checked.

faq.q: Does honey really work for coughs?
faq.a: In an analysis pooling several studies of children with a sudden cough, honey reduced coughing a little compared with doing nothing. Adults can also try about **a spoonful** in warm water. But **never give it to babies under one year old** (risk of botulism).

faq.q: Can I take a cough suppressant and a mucus thinner together?
faq.a: They work in opposite directions, so as a rule they're not used together. If you have phlegm, take only the mucus thinner; use a cough suppressant only at night when a dry cough keeps you from sleeping. Some multi-symptom cold medicines contain both, so check the ingredient list.

faq.q: My cold is gone, but the cough is still here.
faq.a: A cough after a cold can last **3 weeks, or up to 8 weeks**, because the airways have become oversensitive. If it's been more than 3 weeks, or you have wheezing, blood in your phlegm, weight loss or drenching night sweats, asthma, reflux or tuberculosis need to be checked, so see a doctor.

dyspepsia.lead: For bloating after overeating or greasy food, digestive enzymes are the right fit; if the pit of your stomach burns or hurts, it's an acid problem (antacids, famotidine). Pain in the pit of the stomach that doesn't get better after a few days of convenience-store digestive aids could be gastritis, an ulcer, the gallbladder, or even the heart, so get checked.

plan.title: Bloated after overeating — digestive enzymes
plan.why: In Korea, sold even at convenience stores. 1–2 tablets after a meal.

plan.title: Gas and burping — simethicone
plan.why: It pops gas bubbles to let the gas out. It isn't absorbed into your body, so it tends to have few side effects.

plan.title: Burning in the pit of the stomach — antacids, famotidine
plan.why: If it's an acid symptom, digestive aids won't do it.

plan.title: If it's a cramping, wringing pain — trimebutine
plan.why: A twisting pain in your belly is your gut cramping. Trimebutine relaxes that cramping. **You can buy it at a pharmacy.**

plan.title: If it keeps coming back — motility medicine, tests (prescription)
plan.why: Functional dyspepsia is treated with prescription medicine and a test for Helicobacter.

how: After a meal, take 1–2 digestive tablets with warm water and walk gently for just 10 minutes.
If the pit of your stomach burns, switch to an antacid, and if it keeps coming back, take famotidine.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist clearly, “I feel bloated” or “It burns in the pit of my stomach.”
**If you are over 65, be sure to say so.** Some ingredients in digestive aids, and antispasmodics, can cause dry mouth and trouble passing urine in older adults.
selfcare: Eat slowly, in small amounts, and don't lie down right after a meal.
Cut back on fizzy drinks, greasy food and alcohol.
avoid: Don't prick your fingertips or make yourself vomit because you have indigestion. It doesn't help and can injure you.
Don't push through pain in the pit of your stomach with painkillers (anti-inflammatories). They harm your stomach further.

notWorking.title: If the medicine isn't helping much
steps: Pharmacy medicine is normally used for up to 2 weeks. If it hasn't improved after 2 weeks or keeps coming back, have a doctor check for gastritis, an ulcer, or gallbladder problems — if you have Helicobacter, you may need treatment to get rid of it (your doctor decides).
Be sure to see a doctor if you are losing weight, have black stools or trouble swallowing, develop indigestion for the first time after age 40, or have indigestion that keeps going on.

faq.q: Can I take a digestive aid and an antacid together?
faq.a: They're different types, so you can take them together. But choosing by symptom comes first — for bloating and burping, **digestive enzymes or simethicone**; for burning in the pit of the stomach, **antacids or famotidine**. If neither changes anything after a few days, you need tests, not medicine.

faq.q: My upper stomach hurts — could it be my heart?
faq.a: If you are 65 or older, or have diabetes, smoke, or have high blood pressure, heart pain can come on **like indigestion**. If it gets worse when you walk or climb stairs, or comes with cold sweats or pain spreading to your left arm, jaw or back, don't take a digestive aid — **call 119**.

faq.q: Is lying down right after eating a problem?
faq.a: Yes. Don't lie down for 2–3 hours after eating, eat small amounts often rather than a lot at once, and cut back on greasy food, alcohol and late-night snacks — these are the first steps for indigestion that keeps coming back. If it still keeps coming back for more than 2 weeks after doing this, consider an upper endoscopy.

diarrhea.lead:
Diarrhea that starts suddenly is usually viral or from spoiled food, and the treatment isn't medicine but **water and electrolytes**.

For watery diarrhea without fever or blood, an anti-diarrhea medicine (loperamide) shortens it a little. But **if you have a fever or blood or mucus in your stool**, it can keep germs in the gut, so it isn't used. That's why doctors don't prescribe anti-diarrhea medicine alone for long either.

If you have a fever or blood or mucus in your stool, **do not take** anti-diarrhea medicine — see a doctor first.
diarrhea.planLabel: Fluids come 1st; medicine only in some cases

plan.title: Drink often — this is the treatment
plan.why:
The first thing is to replace the water and salt you lose with diarrhea. The trick is **a cup each time you have diarrhea**, sipping little and often.

**The 1st choice is oral rehydration solution from the pharmacy.** It has salt and sugar in the right ratio for absorption, so the water actually gets taken in. In studies against the older formula, it shortened diarrhea by about 1/4 of a day, and fewer people needed IV fluids.

**If you can't get it,** dilute a sports drink about half and half with water. Plain water alone dilutes the salt in your body.

plan.title: Don't fast — keep filling up with plain rice porridge and water while it clears out
plan.why:
Fasting when you have diarrhea actually slows recovery. **Just avoid spicy, salty and greasy food**, and keep eating gentle things like plain rice porridge and thin rice gruel along with water.

**Eating while letting the stool pass** is the way to recover — not forcing the gut to stop.

plan.title: Smectite — holds things in the gut without stopping it
plan.why: It **absorbs** toxins and water in the gut and firms up the stool. Because it doesn't stop the gut from moving, **there's less worry about trapping germs.** That's why it's worth trying before an anti-diarrhea medicine. Take it two hours apart from other medicines. **It's for adults only** — the current package insert says not to use it in children (for children's diarrhea, fluids and electrolytes and a doctor come first).

plan.title: If your belly cramps with it — trimebutine
plan.why: A twisting pain during diarrhea is your gut cramping. Trimebutine **evens out gut movement** (package insert: digestive problems such as belly pain, irritable bowel, and diarrhea not caused by infection). **You can take it with smectite — just space them two hours apart.** It fills the same slot as the antispasmodics doctors prescribe, and **you can buy it at a pharmacy.**

plan.title: Only when you really must stop it — loperamide
plan.why:
For watery diarrhea without fever or blood, an anti-diarrhea medicine (loperamide) shortens it a little. But **if you have a fever or blood or mucus in your stool**, it can keep germs in the gut, so it isn't used. That's why doctors don't prescribe anti-diarrhea medicine alone for long either.

So use it only briefly, **when you have a reason it must stop, like having to go out today**. If you have a fever or bloody stool, **never use it.** On your own judgment, don't use it for more than two days.

plan.title: If you're taking antibiotics — probiotics
plan.why:
For diarrhea that starts while you're on antibiotics, **probiotics** have the best evidence. In an analysis pooling several studies, **when 6–9 people use them, about 1 benefits**.

**Take them 2–3 hours apart from the antibiotic** — swallowed together, the antibiotic kills the probiotic bacteria first. Keep taking them for a few days after you stop the antibiotic.

plan.title: If you have fever and pain — acetaminophen
plan.why: Your gut is sensitive right now, so avoid anti-inflammatories and use **acetaminophen**. Doctors also use acetaminophen when a stomach bug needs pain or fever relief.

plan.title: What doctors do — the clinic diarrhea combination
plan.why:
**Rifaximin** — an antibiotic that's barely absorbed and works only inside the gut, so it's used first.
**Antispasmodics such as trimebutine** — for cramping belly pain.
Mosapride — when your stomach feels bloated and food won't go down.
Acetaminophen — for fever and pain.

If, after eating food that spoils easily such as sea urchin, **the fever rises and dehydration is clear**, doctors treat it as bacterial and move to **ciprofloxacin**. If you're dizzy and your mouth is dry, getting IV fluids is much faster.

how: Each time you have diarrhea, drink a cup of water and oral rehydration solution. Keep going until your urine turns pale.
Eat soft foods like porridge, bananas, white rice and toast, and avoid milk and greasy food for a while.
Take anti-diarrhea medicine (loperamide) only when there's no fever or bloody stool, and for no more than 2 days.
pharmacy: First tell the pharmacist, “I have no fever or blood in my stool (or: I do).” Whether you can be given anti-diarrhea medicine depends on this.
If you're taking antibiotics, be sure to say so. The diarrhea may be caused by the antibiotic.
selfcare: Drink water little and often. Oral rehydration solution (electrolyte replacement) from the pharmacy is best.
Wash your hands often. It keeps you from passing it to your family.
Probiotics (Lactobacillus rhamnosus GG, Saccharomyces boulardii) have evidence for preventing diarrhea caused by antibiotics.
avoid: Don't use anti-diarrhea medicine for diarrhea with fever or blood. It traps the germs in your body.
Don't give anti-diarrhea medicine to babies or young children.
Taking anti-inflammatories when you're dehydrated harms your kidneys.

notWorking.title: If the medicine isn't helping much
steps: See a doctor if it lasts more than two days, you go more than 6 times a day, or you pass less urine and feel dizzy (dehydration).
For bloody stool, high fever, or severe belly pain, get seen right away.

faq.q: Can I replace fluids with a sports drink?
faq.a: Sports drinks are **high in sugar and low in electrolytes**, so they can make diarrhea more watery. Mix them with an equal amount of water, or best of all, use **oral rehydration solution (electrolyte powder)** from the pharmacy. People 65 and older become dehydrated quickly, so act right away if urine gets darker.

faq.q: Should I fast when I have diarrhea?
faq.a: No. If you can eat, eat — start with soft things like porridge, rice, bananas and boiled potatoes. Cut back on dairy, greasy food, coffee and alcohol for a few days. Fasting actually slows your gut's recovery.

faq.q: Do probiotics help?
faq.a: Keep your expectations low. For sudden diarrhea in adults, a recent analysis pooling several studies changed its conclusion, finding it hard to say that probiotics shorten diarrhea. They're not harmful, but they can't replace water and electrolytes.

allergy.lead: For hives, itching and an allergic runny nose, one 2nd-generation antihistamine a day is the basic choice. **In the daytime, loratadine or fexofenadine; if effect comes first, cetirizine (at bedtime)**. If your lips or eyes swell or you're short of breath, you need the emergency room, not medicine.

plan.title: Without drowsiness — loratadine / fexofenadine
plan.why: For driving or work. Don't take fexofenadine with fruit juice or antacids.

plan.title: Effect first — cetirizine
plan.why: One of the strongest of the 2nd generation; take it at bedtime.

plan.title: Bug bites or itching in one spot — medicine you put on the skin
plan.why: Steroid or antihistamine creams you put on the skin (pharmacy). Try not to scratch.

plan.title: 6 weeks or more, or severe — see a doctor
plan.why: Long-lasting hives: a higher antihistamine dose (by a doctor) and tests. Allergy tests to find the cause.

how: Take loratadine 10 mg once in the morning, or cetirizine 10 mg once before bed. While symptoms keep coming back, you can take it every day.
Put a cold compress on itchy spots.
pharmacy: Tell the pharmacist whether you need to drive or work, about any kidney or liver disease or pregnancy, and which cold medicines you take.
**If hives spread all over your body and your lips or eyes swell or you're short of breath,** you need the emergency room, not a pharmacy. Say that first.
selfcare: Wash with lukewarm water and apply plenty of moisturizer. Avoid tight clothes.
Write down new foods or medicines you've had and new things that touched your skin. They're the key to finding the cause.
avoid: Taking a cold medicine that contains chlorpheniramine together with an antihistamine allergy medicine doubles up the antihistamine.
Washing with hot water or scratching makes the itching worse.

notWorking.title: If the medicine isn't helping much
steps: Try switching to cetirizine or taking it in the evening.
If it keeps coming back for more than 6 weeks, it's long-lasting hives. Have a doctor adjust the dose and run tests.
If your lips or eyes swell or your breathing feels tight, it's an emergency. Call 119 right away.

faq.q: Can I take antihistamines for a long time?
faq.a: With 2nd-generation ones (loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine), it's common to take them every day for months for long-lasting hives. But if you are over 65, watch for drowsiness and falls with cetirizine, and if your kidneys are weak, the dose needs to be lowered.

faq.q: Can I put steroid cream on hives?
faq.a: Hives are swelling deep in the skin, so **creams do very little**. An antihistamine you swallow is the answer. Creams are for when the surface is red and itchy, like eczema or a bug bite.

faq.q: How can I tell if it's a food allergy?
faq.a: Suspect it if hives, lip swelling or vomiting keep happening **within 2 hours** of eating. Write down what you ate and when, and get allergy testing. If you're short of breath or your voice changes, call 119 right away.
